interviewQuestions.question: How would you write a Sudoku solver?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as backtracking search: find the next empty cell, try each legal digit 1-9 in it, recurse, and undo if the recursive call fails to reach a full solution. Base case: no empty cells left means the board is solved, return true.

The part worth being explicit about is how "legal" gets checked. Rather than scanning up to 9 cells in the row, 9 in the column, and 9 in the box on every trial digit, I'd maintain nine row sets, nine column sets, and nine box sets of digits already placed — checking legality becomes three O(1) set-membership tests, and placing or undoing a digit just adds or removes it from those three sets.

A concrete trace: at an empty cell in row 2, column 4, box 1, I'd try digit 5 by checking `5 not in rows[2]`, `5 not in cols[4]`, `5 not in boxes[1]` — all three must hold before placing it.

This alone solves any valid Sudoku correctly. Whether it solves it *fast enough* on genuinely hard puzzles is a separate question — that's where cell-selection ordering (which cell to try next, not just which digit) becomes the real lever, which I'd get into if asked to optimize.

**Testing:** whether you can produce a correct backtracking solver with O(1) legality checks, the expected baseline for this problem.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Your Sudoku solver is correct but takes several seconds on genuinely hard puzzles. How would you speed it up?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The single biggest lever is **which empty cell to fill next**, not the digit-legality check itself. A fixed top-left-to-bottom-right scan is correct but can branch very widely on an early cell that still has 6-7 legal candidates, and most of that branching turns out to be wasted once a more-constrained cell elsewhere rules things out.

I'd apply the **minimum-remaining-values (MRV)** heuristic: always fill the empty cell with the fewest legal candidates left, not the first one found. A cell down to one option is effectively forced — filling it immediately propagates that constraint outward before the search commits to any wide, uncertain branch. This means maintaining a live count of legal candidates per empty cell, updated whenever a neighboring row, column, or box gets a new digit.

Concretely, after placing a digit, I'd update the candidate counts for every cell in that same row, column, and box — those are the only cells that could possibly have changed. That's constraint propagation: eliminations happen proactively at placement time, not lazily only when a cell is finally visited.

Together, MRV plus propagation is often the difference between a solver that struggles on a genuinely hard, near-worst-case puzzle and one that solves it in milliseconds — correctness is identical either way, only search efficiency changes.

**Testing:** whether you know MRV and propagation by name and mechanism, the standard senior-level answer to "make backtracking faster."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Optimization

interviewQuestions.question: How is Sudoku an instance of a more general problem type, and why does that framing matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Sudoku is a **constraint satisfaction problem (CSP)**: a set of variables (the empty cells), each with a domain of legal values (digits not yet ruled out), linked by constraints (row/column/box uniqueness) that a full assignment has to satisfy simultaneously. Framed that way, the *solving technique* — backtracking search, most-constrained-variable-first ordering, propagating eliminations after each assignment — isn't specific to Sudoku at all.

Map coloring fits the identical template: variables are regions, domain is the set of colors, constraint is "adjacent regions must differ." Cryptarithmetic puzzles fit it too: variables are letters, domain is 0-9, constraint is the arithmetic equation holding (plus no leading zero). Scheduling problems — assign time slots to tasks subject to resource and ordering constraints — are CSPs as well.

The value of recognizing this in an interview: if you're handed an unfamiliar constraint-shaped problem, you don't need to invent a new algorithm from scratch. You map it onto variables/domains/constraints, apply the same backtracking-plus-MRV-plus-propagation toolkit, and adapt only the constraint-checking function to the new problem's specific rules — the search structure transfers directly.

**Testing:** whether you can generalize a specific algorithm into a reusable pattern, which is exactly the kind of abstraction a staff-level candidate is expected to make.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Generalization

interviewQuestions.question: Your Sudoku solver re-validates the entire board after every single digit placement to make sure nothing's broken. Is that necessary, and what would you change?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's not necessary, and I'd change it, because placing one digit at a specific `(row, col)` can only possibly create a new conflict within that digit's own row, its own column, and its own 3x3 box — every other row, column, and box is provably untouched by that single placement and doesn't need re-checking at all.

Re-validating the whole board turns what should be a cheap, localized check into an O(81) scan, paid on every trial digit at every cell throughout the entire search — that cost compounds badly across a search that might try thousands of digit placements before finding (or failing to find) a solution.

The fix mirrors the same idea as the O(1) legality checks generally: maintain row/column/box sets of placed digits, and when placing or undoing a digit, only touch the three sets it actually belongs to. Checking legality then only ever needs to look at those same three sets — no board-wide scan, ever, at any point in the algorithm.

I'd point out this is the same class of bug as N-Queens' board-rescan-per-placement inefficiency — correct, but paying for global information that a placement could only ever affect locally. Recognizing "what could this change have possibly affected" is the general debugging instinct that applies here.

**Testing:** whether you can localize the blast radius of a single mutation instead of defaulting to a full re-check, a common real-world performance bug pattern.
